Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment Sign up for our free newsletter here And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager . Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth , coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it. But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth…

guardianfootball.description: Gli Azzurri show positive signs of improvement in seesaw 3-3 draw against a Roma side inspired by Messi-like Matías Soulé Scott McTominay was leaving nothing to doubt. He appeared to have scored with a close-range header early in the second half of Napoli’s game at home to Roma, but Pierluigi Gollini clawed the ball out from inside the goal. McTominay got his noggin to the rebound, nudging it back across the line. Roma’s keeper pushed away again, so the Napoli midfielder got to his feet and smashed a shot into the back of the net. Just typical. You wait two months for your first goal of the Serie A season, then three show up at once. They only counted for one, of course, but McTominay…

The Cherries are smart at investing, far more so than Manchester United, who have wasted a lot of money by failing to look outside the box for players like Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson. United may not have the wealth they previously showed in the transfer market but Bournemouth are showing what can be done within a budget and, more importantly, will be able to make a profit on signings. guardianfootball.description: Thirteen years later, José Mourinho led Real Madrid into the Camp Nou as one team and them out again as another having secured the kind of late victory he loves and which opens up a whole new world. With just three minutes and the final reserves of energy remaining, a wonderful moment of skill from Jude Bellingham found Eduardo Camavinga and set them on one last run. Camavinga sprinted free, skilfully slipped Pau Cubarsí and pulled back for Kylian Mbappé to provide the finish, a little bit of history written. “The world that loves football will have stopped to watch this and they won’t have gone disappointed; this was two teams that played to win,” Mourinho said. It had been an intense,…

guardianfootball.description: At long last, a weakness has been spotted. Finally, the 100% winning start ends for Manchester City, much to the pleasure of Manchester United, who struck late through Elisabeth Terland to claim a point in a well-contested and at times breathless derby. Khadija “Bunny” Shaw’s second-half strike – her 91st WSL goal on her 100th appearance in the division – appeared to have settled the game and kept the defending champions top of the table, and it had looked likely to be the same old story, of City finding a way to win a game that was on a knife-edge, because they have the game’s deadliest finisher. Continue reading...

quietus.title: The Strange World Of… Jennifer Walshe
quietus.description: Ahead of her curation of this year's Deep Time Festival, the Irish experimentalist gives Alastair Shuttleworth 10 entry points into a back catalogue which includes an opera with Barbie dolls, 12 fictional aliases and a board game for them to play Jennifer Walshe by Blackie Bouffant Flann O’Brien, one of Jennifer Walshe’s favourite Irish writers, once wrote of speaking Irish “when it was neither profitable nor popular.” Walshe has been ahead of the curve herself in speaking about the rise of AI, which brought her career-spanning questions about art, truth and technology into focus. A prolific improviser, composer and researcher, she is one of the most celebrated figures working in…

quietus.title: Oliver Leith – Doom and the Dooms
quietus.description: Oliver Leith Doom and the Dooms Based on transcriptions direct from tapes found at a jumble sale, the latest from Oliver Leith may be the ideal entry point to the British composer's oeuvre Steady pulse, parallel melodies. Strings undulating with opulent vibrato. Percussive garnish that, clinking and clattering, sounds just like a five-year-old breaking a piggy bank. Endless vacillation between hope and despair. Endless vacillation between stately ceremony and soft frolicking. All processed as if through a stereo-widening plug-in. This is Oliver Leith’s signature style, and it’s easy to start taking it for granted – mostly because of how effortless he makes it sound. Commissioned by Wigmore…

quietus.title: Kevin Martin Blocks Unlicensed GOD Reissue
quietus.description: He revealed that he is now in talks with a record label to produce an official box set of the group's material Kevin Martin has taken to Instagram to reveal that he's successfully blocked an unlicensed reissue of Possession, a 1992 album by GOD, the band that he was part of from 1987 until 1996. Updating his social media followers, Martin thanked people who had offered him legal advice on the matter and said he'd fought back against the planned reissue on "legal and moral grounds". He added that the process of blocking the release had been "difficult and stressful", but ultimately successful, and that none of the members of GOD had approved the reissue. The dispute was over a planned new…

Claire Biddles & Fergal Kinney deal with an LP which is experimental outlier, outsider art & baffling mess all at once There’s a moment in 2016 captured in Chris Heath’s bestselling journalistic portrait of Robbie Williams where the singer is struggling with his infant child emotionally pushing his father away. “Maybe,” offers his wife Ayda Field-Williams, “she’s finally heard Rudebox.” The September 2006 release of the ‘Rudebox’ single remains the most controversial moment in Robbie Williams career, a turning point that decisively ended his imperial phase as Britain’s biggest pop star that he had…

quietus.title: Low Culture Essay: Sophie Sleigh-Johnson on The Indoor League
quietus.description: Rising Damp expert Sophie Sleigh-Johnson tunes in to the 70s pub sports telly series that celebrated regional specificity through a fug of cig smoke and the rituals of indoor combat Something was afoot in the corridors of Yorkshire TV during the early 70s, fuelled by crates of Double Diamond beer. The chipboard sets of Rising Damp, a luridly claustrophobic set piece transmitted into the country’s living rooms, shared production space (if not a specific studio) at Kirkstall Road Studios, Leeds with another domesticated strain of British culture: the pub. Long before Luke Littler brought darts to the TikTok generation and Sky homogenised the arrows’ presentation, The Indoor League brought…

quietus.title: Shit And Shine – 0 aa Riot
quietus.description: Shit And Shine 0 aa Riot The ever-prolific Craig Clouse gives us four tracks of skipping needles and sporadic glitches, but it's the subtle details and small shifts that prove most beguiling for JR Moores 0 aa RIOT by SHIT AND SHINE Paul Du Noyer compared Paul McCartney’s “stylistic breadth” to Pablo Picasso. Will Gompertz eulogised David Bowie as “the Picasso of pop”. Leonard Cohen saw Bob Dylan as “the Picasso” and considered himself a lower-rung Matisse. Kanye West and Madonna have likened themselves to the great master. Mike Skinner said he was “the Pablo Picasso of geezer garage”. Notwithstanding this painter’s stranglehold over Western aesthetic thinking and ignoring his personal…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Willis Alan Ramsey :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: More than 50 years after releasing one of the great cult albums of the early ’70s, Willis Alan Ramsey remains an enigma: a singular songwriter whose long-awaited second record has yet to materialize. But as a recent live appearance and a first-ever vinyl reissue of his self-titled debut attest, Ramsey is very much still here — and already thinking beyond the follow-up he once abandoned. We caught up with the Texas songwriter to talk about the making of a classic, the decades since, and the music still to come.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Surprise Chef :: Frogs In A Pond
aquariumdrunkard.description: Like the best giallo scores, Surprise Chef's Frogs In A Pond finds beauty in the uneasy marriage of the sinister and the seductive. Its analog warmth and locked-in grooves evoke a bygone era without becoming trapped in it, blurring the line between recordings from 2026 and 1976. The eerie mood of the compositions, mixed with the 8-track recording, creates an auditory twilight zone that’s both nostalgic and immediate.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders :: (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
aquariumdrunkard.description: This Halloween when the usual horror soundtrack fare begins to feel a little too familiar, there is Valerie and Her Week of Wonders. Released in 1970, Jaromil Jireš’s surreal Czech fairy tale is a bizarre, beautiful collision of vampires, witchcraft, religious repression, erotic awakening and dream logic. Paired with Luboš Fišer’s score, the whole thing feels like an intermittent phantasmagoria.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Videodrome :: Psycho II (1983)
aquariumdrunkard.description: About midway through Psycho II (1983), you realize you’re not watching a horror sequel, but a carefully constructed character study. Psycho II isn’t really interested in being a sequel or a horror film; it’s interested in the rehabilitation of Norman Bates, and how those in Bates’ orbit react to that. We may have entered the film expecting a boogeyman, but instead we’re watching a fatally flawed hero, and…we’re rooting for him? Yes, we’re actually rooting for Norman Bates.

aquariumdrunkard.title: A La Altura: Visionary Mexican Music 1977-1999
aquariumdrunkard.description: Experimental music history is still, in large part, a Euro-American project. Rare are the efforts that highlight Latin American pioneers like Beatriz Ferreyra or Jocy de Oliveira, and rarer still are histories of electronic scenes with a pop, new age edge. A La Altura: Visionary Mexican Music 1977-1999 excavates the ambient underground of Mexico City, tracing a vibrant, largely overlooked circuit of independent cassette culture, dubbed tapes, and street stalls. Compiled by Carlos Icaza and Mark McNeill after a decade of research into the city’s cassette history, it offers a long-overdue portrait of Mexico’s experimental music underground.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Chris Lyons :: New Love for the Old Flame
aquariumdrunkard.description: After a pair of excellent albums fronting his New Orleans quartet Silver Synthetic, last year's Painters Street saw musician and vocalist Chris Lyons venturing into promising solo pathways. On sophomore record New Love for the Old Flame , Lyons presents a dazzling collection hovering like the forlorn days of the golden AM dial. The comfort of a lazy afternoon personified in sound.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Jimmy Webb :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: Jimmy Webb has written some of the great songs in the modern American songbook. After turning 80 in August, he's releasing Yours For The Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb , via the revived Sun Records. Featuring guests like Michael McDonald, Graham Nash, and Amy Grant, the new album features both new recordings of long lost songs and original demos. With songs that stretch back across the decades, it's a collection that showcases Webb's mastery. He joins us to discuss the magic of a song demo, his upbringing in the church, and his lifelong love of science fiction.
